opus-5.5.text:
What strikes me most is that the model doesn't do addition the way we were taught in school. You might expect it to have memorized a giant lookup table, or to have learned the carry-the-one algorithm and run it step by step. Instead, when we traced what happens for something like 36 plus 59, we found it splits the work into parallel paths.

One path is fuzzy and approximate. It works out roughly how big the answer is, something like "this is in the high eighties or low nineties." The other path is very precise but narrow: it only cares about the last digit. It has learned that a number ending in 6 plus a number ending in 9 gives a number ending in 5. Then these paths combine. The rough magnitude and the exact ones digit together pin down 95.

Part of why that's so striking is that nobody designed it. The model came up with a strategy of its own that's distinct from the human algorithm, and it's sort of elegant. It's a bit like how you might sanity-check an answer in your head: you get a ballpark and then nail down the details.

The other thing that really got us was what happened when we asked the model how it did the addition. It described the standard schoolbook method: add the ones, carry the one, and so on. So there's a gap between the explanation it gives and the computation actually happening inside. That makes sense if you think about it. It learned to explain math from human-written text, where people describe the carry algorithm, but it learned to actually *do* math through a different process entirely. That's a nice concrete example of why interpretability matters. You can't always take the model's self-report at face value, and having tools that look at the internals directly lets you check.

And then there's reuse. Some of these features, like the ones for adding numbers that end in particular digits, aren't specific to arithmetic problems. They fire in other contexts too, like working out dates or totals in a table. So the model seems to have built general components it reuses wherever they're useful, which says something interesting about how these systems generalize.

r001.rationale: The response says Claude does not use the taught carry-the-one method, instead combining parallel paths, and calls its strategy distinct from the human algorithm.

r002.rationale: It describes a precise path that determines the last digit, giving 6 plus 9 as producing a number ending in 5.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so what really struck me was that it's doing two things at once, in parallel, and neither of them is what you'd write down if you were doing it by hand. We looked at a case like 36 plus 59, and if you trace the circuit, you don't find the model carrying the one from the ones column the way you learned in school. Instead there's one set of features doing a kind of rough, fuzzy estimate of the magnitude of the answer, something like "this is going to be in the high eighties or nineties," and then a separate set of features that are very precise about the last digit. They know that six plus nine ends in five, basically a lookup on the ones digits modulo ten. And then those two pathways get combined at the end to produce 95.

So it's a parallel approximate-plus-exact strategy, which is kind of elegant, and it's not something anyone taught it. It just emerged because that's a convenient way to get the right answer in a fixed number of layers.

The other thing that I find really fun is that if you then ask Claude how it did the addition, it tells you the schoolbook story. It says, "I added the ones digits, carried the one, added the tens." And that's just not what we see inside. It's not lying exactly, it's giving the explanation it learned from humans explaining addition. So there's this gap between the mechanism and the introspective report, and that was one of the clearest examples we had that you can't fully trust the model's account of its own reasoning. You have to actually look.

r001.rationale: It says Claude does not carry the one as taught in school and instead uses a parallel approximate-plus-exact strategy.

r002.rationale: It says a separate pathway precisely determines the last digit by adding the ones digits modulo ten.

astra-6.text:
What I find striking is that it doesn’t seem to use just one clean, sequential algorithm, like the way we’re taught to add numbers on paper. There are multiple computations happening in parallel. Some are tracking the rough magnitude of the answer, while others are working out more precise information, like what the last digit should be. Those pieces come together to produce the answer.

So even though we call it a single forward pass, that doesn’t mean it’s a single operation. There’s a lot of internal structure and computation across the layers. And the interesting thing is that the procedure we uncover isn’t necessarily the procedure the model describes if you ask it how it did the addition.

r001.rationale: It contrasts Claude’s parallel internal computations with the clean, sequential paper addition method taught in school.

r002.rationale: It says some computations work out precise information, including what the sum’s last digit should be.

sol-6.1.text:
What’s striking is that a single forward pass doesn’t mean a single operation. There’s a lot of computation happening across layers, and different parts of the model can contribute different pieces of the answer.

So you might imagine a clean algorithm: add the ones, carry the one, add the tens. But the internal picture is more distributed. There can be pathways working out particular digits, pathways handling carries, and pathways producing a rough sense of the magnitude of the result. Those signals come together to determine the answer.

That’s interesting because the model can produce something that looks like a familiar, sequential calculation through a collection of computations that are partly happening in parallel. And explaining the calculation in words afterward is a separate process from the computation that actually produced it.

r001.rationale: It contrasts the familiar sequential addition algorithm with Claude’s more distributed, partly parallel internal computation.

r002.rationale: It mentions pathways handling particular digits, but does not clearly state that Claude’s computation precisely determines the sum’s final digit.
